theorems.name: Principle of Variation and Natural Selection
theorems.statement: Individuals in a population differ from one another; some of these differences are heritable. Individuals with variations better suited to their environment survive and reproduce more successfully, so those traits become more common over generations.

theorems.name: DNA Double Helix and Complementary Base Pairing
theorems.statement: DNA is a double helix in which adenine pairs with thymine and guanine pairs with cytosine. Each strand can act as a template for a new strand, allowing genetic information to be copied faithfully; rare copying errors generate variation.

misconceptions: All organisms reproduce only sexually — FALSE: bacteria, Hydra, yeast, Spirogyra, and many plants reproduce asexually.
Asexual reproduction creates lots of genetic variation — FALSE: offspring are generally genetically similar to the parent; variation arises mainly from mutations.
Regeneration is the same as reproduction — FALSE: regeneration repairs lost body parts and is not the normal way most organisms produce offspring.
Pollination is the same as fertilisation — FALSE: pollination transfers pollen to the stigma, while fertilisation is the fusion of male and female gametes.
A seed and a fruit are the same thing — FALSE: the seed develops from the ovule, while the fruit develops from the ovary.
Menstruation means a woman is pregnant — FALSE: menstruation occurs when the egg is not fertilised and the uterine lining is shed.

workedExamples.title: Identifying modes of asexual reproduction
workedExamples.problem: Name the mode of asexual reproduction in (i) Hydra, (ii) Spirogyra, (iii) Rhizopus, and (iv) potato, and state one key feature of each mode.
steps: Step 1: Hydra reproduces by budding. A small outgrowth called a bud develops on the parent body.
Step 2: The bud grows, develops tentacles, and detaches as a new individual.
Step 3: Spirogyra reproduces by fragmentation. Its filament breaks into pieces, and each piece grows into a new filament.
Step 4: Rhizopus reproduces by spore formation. Spores are produced inside sporangia at the tips of hyphae.
Step 5: When the sporangium bursts, spores are dispersed and germinate in suitable conditions.
Step 6: Potato reproduces vegetatively through eyes (buds) on its tuber; each eye can grow into a new plant.
Step 7: All four modes involve a single parent and no fusion of gametes, so they are asexual.
workedExamples.shortcut: Asexual reproduction is usually recognised by one parent, no gamete fusion, and offspring that are genetically very similar to the parent.

workedExamples.title: Binary fission in Amoeba
workedExamples.problem: Describe binary fission in Amoeba with the help of a sequence of stages.
steps: Step 1: The parent Amoeba is a single cell with a nucleus and organelles.
Step 2: The nucleus divides first by mitosis, producing two nuclei.
Step 3: The cytoplasm then divides, and the cell membrane pinches inward.
Step 4: Two daughter cells are formed, each with one nucleus.
Step 5: The daughter cells are genetically similar to the parent.
Step 6: Under favourable conditions, Amoeba can divide repeatedly, producing a large population.
workedExamples.shortcut: Binary fission gives two daughter cells; multiple fission gives many daughter cells, as in Plasmodium.

workedExamples.title: From pollination to seed formation
workedExamples.problem: Trace the events in a flowering plant from pollination to the formation of a seed and fruit.
steps: Step 1: Pollen grains land on the stigma of a compatible flower; this is pollination.
Step 2: A pollen grain germinates and forms a pollen tube that grows through the style towards the ovary.
Step 3: The pollen tube carries two male gametes into the ovule.
Step 4: One male gamete fuses with the egg to form a zygote; this is fertilisation.
Step 5: The second male gamete fuses with the polar nuclei to form the primary endosperm nucleus; this is double fertilisation.
Step 6: The zygote develops into an embryo, and the ovule develops into a seed.
Step 7: The ovary develops into the fruit, and the ovary wall becomes the pericarp.
Step 8: The seed contains the embryo and stored food and can germinate into a new plant under suitable conditions.
workedExamples.shortcut: Double fertilisation is a feature of flowering plants: one male gamete forms the zygote, the other forms the endosperm.

science:heredity-and-evolution.title: Heredity and Evolution — Student Knowledge Hub for India

outcomes: Distinguish inherited traits from acquired traits and explain the role of variation
State and apply Mendel's laws of dominance, segregation, and independent assortment
Solve monohybrid and dihybrid crosses using correct Punnett squares and ratios
Explain sex determination in humans and identify the role of the father
Evaluate fossils, homologous organs, and analogous organs as evidence for evolution
Explain speciation through reproductive isolation and describe broad trends in human evolution
Explain and apply Heredity and Evolution.

concepts.name: Variation and Acquired versus Inherited Traits
concepts.purpose: Variation is the difference in characteristics among individuals of the same species. It arises mainly from the recombination of genes during sexual reproduction, from small errors made while DNA is copied, and from the mixing of parental genes. Inherited traits are controlled by genes in the germ cells and are passed from parents to offspring. Acquired traits, such as a scar, a learned skill, or muscles built by exercise, arise during an individual's lifetime and generally do not alter the DNA of germ cells, so they are not passed on.
concepts.realLife: Siblings differ in height, eye colour and face shape because each receives a different combination of parental genes, while a childhood scar is not passed on to their children.

concepts.name: Mendel's Monohybrid Cross: Dominance and Segregation
concepts.purpose: Mendel crossed true-breeding tall and dwarf pea plants and obtained only tall plants in the F1 generation. When the F1 plants were self-pollinated, the dwarf trait reappeared in the F2 generation in a 3 tall : 1 dwarf ratio. This showed that the tall allele is dominant, that the dwarf allele remains hidden in F1, and that the two alleles of a gene separate during gamete formation.
concepts.realLife: A pure tall pea plant crossed with a pure dwarf plant gives tall plants in the first generation, but dwarf plants can reappear in the next generation, which is why breeders keep pedigree records.

concepts.name: Dihybrid Cross and Independent Assortment
concepts.purpose: A dihybrid cross follows two pairs of contrasting traits at the same time, such as seed shape and seed colour. Mendel crossed round yellow seeds with wrinkled green seeds and obtained round yellow plants in F1. Self-pollination of F1 gave four phenotypic classes in the ratio 9 : 3 : 3 : 1. This result supports the law of independent assortment: the alleles of one gene separate independently of the alleles of another gene during gamete formation.
concepts.realLife: Plant breeders combine two useful traits, such as high yield and disease resistance, by crossing parents and selecting the desired combinations in later generations.

concepts.name: Sex Determination in Humans
concepts.purpose: In humans, sex is determined by a pair of sex chromosomes. A female has two X chromosomes (XX) and a male has one X and one Y chromosome (XY). The mother always contributes an X chromosome, while the father contributes either an X or a Y chromosome. Therefore the sex of the child is determined by the father's sperm, and the chance of a boy or a girl is about one in two for each pregnancy.
concepts.realLife: Parents who already have daughters sometimes believe the next child must be a boy, but each pregnancy is an independent event with the same roughly equal chance.

concepts.name: Evidence for Evolution: Fossils, Homologous and Analogous Organs
concepts.purpose: Evolution is the gradual change in the inherited characteristics of populations over many generations. Fossils are remains or impressions of past organisms preserved in rocks, and they show that life forms have changed over time. Homologous organs have the same basic structure and origin but may perform different functions, which suggests common ancestry. Analogous organs have different structures and origins but perform similar functions, which suggests convergent evolution rather than close relationship.
concepts.realLife: The forelimbs of a frog, lizard, bird and human have the same basic bone plan but are used for jumping, running, flying and writing, which points to a shared ancestor.

concepts.name: Speciation and Human Evolution
concepts.purpose: A new species forms when populations of the same species become reproductively isolated and accumulate enough genetic differences that they can no longer interbreed. Geographical isolation, such as a river, mountain range or sea, is a common starting point, and genetic drift and natural selection then act on the separated populations. Human evolution follows the same broad principles: fossil and molecular evidence show that modern humans share a common ancestor with other primates and that features such as bipedalism, larger brains and tool use appeared gradually.
concepts.realLife: Island populations of birds and lizards often differ from mainland relatives because they have been isolated for long periods and have evolved separately.

mindMap.title: Heredity and Evolution - Mind Map

keyPoints: Variation and Acquired versus Inherited Traits
Mendel's Monohybrid Cross: Dominance and Segregation
Evidence for Evolution: Fossils, Homologous and Analogous Organs
misconceptions: Acquired traits are inherited - FALSE: acquired changes occur in somatic cells and generally do not alter germ-cell DNA.
The dominant allele is the one that is more common in the population - FALSE: dominance describes expression in a heterozygote, not frequency.
A 3:1 ratio means that every family of four children must have three tall and one dwarf - FALSE: the ratio is a probability seen over many offspring, not a guarantee for a small family.
Every tall pea plant is TT - FALSE: a tall plant can be TT or Tt.
The mother determines the sex of the child - FALSE: the mother gives only X, while the father gives X or Y.
Homologous organs must perform the same function - FALSE: homologous organs share structure and origin but often perform different functions.

quickCheck.question: What is the unit of heredity?
quickCheck.explanation: A gene is a segment of DNA that controls a trait and is the unit of heredity.

quickCheck.question: Mendel carried out his experiments on which plant?
quickCheck.explanation: Mendel used the garden pea, Pisum sativum, because it has clear contrasting traits and can be cross-pollinated.

quickCheck.question: A dominant allele is expressed when it is present in:
quickCheck.explanation: A dominant allele is expressed even in the heterozygous condition, so one copy is enough.

quickCheck.question: The genotype of a pure tall pea plant is:
quickCheck.explanation: A pure tall plant has two dominant tall alleles, TT.

revisionPlan: Read the Heredity and Evolution notes and write five key definitions.
Solve three board-style questions and check every step.

workedExamples.title: Monohybrid cross between pure tall and pure dwarf pea plants
workedExamples.problem: A pure tall pea plant (TT) is crossed with a pure dwarf pea plant (tt). Work out the F1 and F2 generations using Punnett squares, and state the genotypic and phenotypic ratios of F2.
steps: Step 1: Assign alleles. Let T be the dominant allele for tallness and t the recessive allele for dwarfness.
Step 2: The parents are TT (tall) and tt (dwarf). Their gametes are T and t respectively.
Step 3: Cross TT with tt. Every F1 offspring receives T from one parent and t from the other, so all F1 plants are Tt.
Step 4: All F1 plants are Tt, and because T is dominant, all F1 plants are tall.
Step 5: Self-pollinate the F1 plants: Tt x Tt. Each parent can form gametes T and t.
Step 6: Draw the 2 x 2 Punnett square with T and t on both sides: TT, Tt, Tt, tt.
Step 7: Count genotypes: 1 TT, 2 Tt and 1 tt. The genotypic ratio is 1 : 2 : 1.
Step 8: Count phenotypes: TT and Tt are tall (3 boxes), while tt is dwarf (1 box). The phenotypic ratio is 3 tall : 1 dwarf.
Step 9: Check that the ratios add up correctly: genotypes 1 + 2 + 1 = 4 boxes, phenotypes 3 + 1 = 4 boxes.

workedExamples.title: Using a test cross to find an unknown genotype
workedExamples.problem: A tall pea plant may be TT or Tt. Explain how a test cross with a dwarf plant can identify its genotype, and predict the offspring in each case.
steps: Step 1: A test cross is a cross of an individual showing the dominant trait with a homozygous recessive individual.
Step 2: Use a dwarf plant of genotype tt as the tester because it can contribute only the recessive allele t.
Step 3: If the tall plant is TT, the cross is TT x tt. All offspring receive T from the tall parent and t from the tester, so all are Tt and all are tall.
Step 4: If the tall plant is Tt, the cross is Tt x tt. The tall parent makes gametes T and t, while the tester makes only t.
Step 5: The Punnett square gives Tt, Tt, tt and tt, so about half the offspring are tall and half are dwarf.
Step 6: The appearance of any dwarf offspring proves that the tall parent carried the recessive allele, so its genotype is Tt.
Step 7: If no dwarf offspring appear in a large sample, the tall parent is probably TT, although a small sample cannot prove it with certainty.

workedExamples.title: Dihybrid cross for seed shape and seed colour
workedExamples.problem: In pea plants, round seed shape (R) is dominant over wrinkled (r), and yellow cotyledon colour (Y) is dominant over green (y). Cross a pure round yellow plant (RRYY) with a pure wrinkled green plant (rryy). Give the F1 genotype and the F2 phenotypic ratio.
steps: Step 1: Assign alleles: R = round, r = wrinkled, Y = yellow, y = green.
Step 2: The parents are RRYY and rryy. Their gametes are RY and ry respectively.
Step 3: All F1 offspring receive R and Y from one parent and r and y from the other, so all are RrYy.
Step 4: Because R and Y are dominant, all F1 seeds are round and yellow.
Step 5: Self-pollinate F1: RrYy x RrYy. Each parent produces four gametes: RY, Ry, rY and ry.
Step 6: Draw a 4 x 4 Punnett square with these four gametes on both edges, giving 16 boxes.
Step 7: Count the phenotypes in the 16 boxes: 9 round yellow, 3 round green, 3 wrinkled yellow and 1 wrinkled green.
Step 8: The F2 phenotypic ratio is therefore 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.
Step 9: The result supports independent assortment because the two gene pairs behave independently when gametes form.

Apply the mirror formula and magnification with the Cartesian sign convention
Explain refraction and use the refractive index to relate speed and bending
Apply the lens formula and magnification for convex and concave lenses
Calculate the power of a lens and the power of lenses in contact
Solve board-style numericals on mirrors, lenses, and refraction
Explain and apply Light - Reflection and Refraction.

concepts.name: Reflection of Light and the Laws of Reflection
concepts.purpose: Light is a form of energy that travels in straight lines in a homogeneous medium. When it strikes a polished surface, it bounces back; this is reflection. The incident ray, the reflected ray, and the normal at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane. The angle of incidence is always equal to the angle of reflection. Regular reflection from a smooth surface gives a clear image, while diffused reflection from a rough surface scatters light in many directions.

concepts.name: Spherical Mirrors and Image Formation
concepts.purpose: A spherical mirror is a part of a hollow sphere whose one surface is silvered. A concave mirror has its reflecting surface curved inward, while a convex mirror has it curved outward. The pole is the centre of the mirror, the centre of curvature is the centre of the sphere, and the principal focus is the point where rays parallel to the principal axis meet or appear to meet after reflection. The focal length is half the radius of curvature, f = R/2 for a mirror of small aperture. Concave mirrors can form real or virtual images, but a convex mirror always forms a virtual, erect, and diminished image.

concepts.name: Mirror Formula and Magnification
concepts.purpose: The mirror formula relates object distance u, image distance v, and focal length f as 1/v + 1/u = 1/f. Distances are measured from the pole using the Cartesian sign convention: distances measured along the incident light are negative, and those measured opposite to it are positive. Magnification is m = -v/u = height of image / height of object. A negative magnification means a real, inverted image, while a positive magnification means a virtual, erect image.

concepts.name: Refraction and Refractive Index
concepts.purpose: Refraction is the bending of light as it passes from one transparent medium to another because its speed changes. When light enters an optically denser medium, it slows down and bends towards the normal; when it enters a rarer medium, it speeds up and bends away from the normal. Snell's law states that sin i / sin r is constant for a given pair of media. The absolute refractive index is n = c/v, where c is the speed of light in vacuum and v is the speed in the medium.

concepts.name: Spherical Lenses and the Lens Formula
concepts.purpose: A lens is a transparent refracting medium bounded by two spherical surfaces. A convex lens is thicker in the middle and converges parallel rays, while a concave lens is thinner in the middle and diverges them. The lens formula is 1/v - 1/u = 1/f, using the same Cartesian sign convention as mirrors. Magnification is m = v/u; a negative m gives a real inverted image and a positive m gives a virtual erect image.

concepts.name: Power of a Lens and Its Applications
concepts.purpose: The power of a lens measures its ability to converge or diverge light and is defined as P = 1/f, where f is the focal length in metres. Its SI unit is the dioptre (D), and 1 D = 1 m^-1. A convex lens has positive power and a concave lens has negative power. When thin lenses are placed in contact, their powers add: P = P1 + P2 + ..., which is used in spectacles and camera lenses.

workedExamples.title: Concave mirror: focal length and magnification
workedExamples.problem: An object is placed 10 cm in front of a concave mirror. A real image is formed 30 cm in front of the mirror. Find the focal length and the magnification.
steps: Step 1: Use the Cartesian sign convention. The object is in front of the mirror, so u = -10 cm.
Step 2: A real image in front of the mirror means v = -30 cm.
Step 3: Apply the mirror formula 1/f = 1/v + 1/u = -1/30 - 1/10.
Step 4: Take a common denominator of 30: -1/30 - 3/30 = -4/30, so f = -7.5 cm.
Step 5: Magnification m = -v/u = -(-30)/(-10) = -3.
Step 6: Negative f confirms a concave mirror; negative m means the image is real, inverted, and 3 times magnified.

workedExamples.title: Convex mirror: image position and nature
workedExamples.problem: An object is placed 15 cm in front of a convex mirror of focal length 10 cm. Find the image distance and magnification.
steps: Step 1: Object distance u = -15 cm and, for a convex mirror, f = +10 cm.
Step 3: Take a common denominator of 30: 3/30 + 2/30 = 5/30 = 1/6.
Step 4: Therefore v = +6 cm. The positive sign means the image is behind the mirror.
Step 6: A positive magnification less than 1 means a virtual, erect, diminished image.

workedExamples.title: Refractive index and speed of light in glass
workedExamples.problem: A ray of light travels from air into glass. The refractive index of glass with respect to air is 1.5 and the speed of light in air is 3 x 10^8 m/s. Find the speed of light in glass and the refractive index of air with respect to glass.
steps: Step 1: Absolute refractive index n = c/v, so v = c/n.
Step 3: The refractive index of air with respect to glass is n_air,glass = n_air / n_glass.
Step 4: Taking n_air = 1, n_air,glass = 1 / 1.5 = 0.67.
Step 5: Light slows down in glass, which is why it bends towards the normal.

Show every step; board marking rewards reasoning.

outcomes: Describe the structure and function of the human eye
Explain accommodation, near point, and far point
Identify myopia, hypermetropia, and presbyopia and calculate correcting lens power
Explain refraction of light through a prism and the angle of deviation

concepts.name: Structure and Working of the Human Eye
concepts.purpose: The human eye is a natural optical instrument shaped almost like a sphere about 2.5 cm in diameter. Light enters through the transparent cornea, passes through the pupil whose size is controlled by the iris, and is focused by the crystalline lens onto the retina. The retina contains light-sensitive cells: rods respond to dim light and cones respond to colour. These cells convert light into electrical signals that travel through the optic nerve to the brain, which interprets the image.

concepts.name: Accommodation, Near Point, and Far Point
concepts.purpose: The eye can focus on objects at different distances by changing the curvature and hence the focal length of its crystalline lens; this ability is called the power of accommodation. The ciliary muscles contract to make the lens thicker and more converging for nearby objects, and relax for distant objects. The near point of a normal adult eye is about 25 cm and the far point is infinity. The range between these limits is called the range of vision.

concepts.name: Defects of Vision and Their Correction
concepts.purpose: Myopia or short-sightedness is the inability to see distant objects clearly; the image of a far object forms in front of the retina. It is corrected by a concave lens of suitable negative power. Hypermetropia or long-sightedness is the inability to see nearby objects clearly; the image forms behind the retina and is corrected by a convex lens of positive power. Presbyopia is the age-related loss of accommodation, caused by weakening of the ciliary muscles and hardening of the lens, and is corrected by bifocal lenses.

concepts.name: Refraction of Light Through a Prism
concepts.purpose: A glass prism is a transparent medium bounded by two triangular bases and three rectangular surfaces. When light passes through a prism, it refracts at both surfaces, and the emergent ray is deviated from the incident direction. The angle between the incident ray and the emergent ray is the angle of deviation. The deviation depends on the angle of the prism, the angle of incidence, and the refractive index of the material.

concepts.name: Dispersion of White Light and the Spectrum
concepts.purpose: White light is a mixture of seven colours: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet. When white light passes through a prism, each colour is refracted by a different amount because the refractive index of glass is different for different colours. Violet bends the most and red the least, so the colours separate into a spectrum. This splitting of white light into its component colours is called dispersion.

concepts.name: Atmospheric Refraction and Scattering of Light
concepts.purpose: The atmosphere is not uniform; its density and refractive index change with height, so light from stars and the Sun bends gradually as it passes through it. This atmospheric refraction causes stars to twinkle and makes the Sun visible a little before actual sunrise and after actual sunset. Scattering of light by molecules and particles makes the sky look blue and the setting Sun look red. The Tyndall effect is the scattering of light by colloidal particles, which makes a beam visible in a dusty room.

workedExamples.title: Myopia: power of the correcting lens
workedExamples.problem: A myopic person can see clearly only up to 80 cm. Find the power of the lens required to correct this defect so that the person can see distant objects clearly.
steps: Step 1: A myopic eye focuses distant objects in front of the retina, so a diverging lens is needed.
Step 2: The lens must form the image of an object at infinity at the far point of the eye, 80 cm in front of the lens.
Step 3: Use u = negative infinity and v = -80 cm = -0.80 m in the lens formula 1/f = 1/v - 1/u.
Step 5: Therefore f = -0.80 m and P = 1/f = -1.25 D.

workedExamples.title: Hypermetropia: power of the correcting lens
workedExamples.problem: A hypermetropic person has a near point of 1 m. Find the power of the lens required to read a book kept at the normal near point of 25 cm.
steps: Step 1: The object is at the normal near point, so u = -25 cm = -0.25 m.
Step 2: The lens must form the image at the person's near point, so v = -1 m.
Step 5: Therefore f = +1/3 m = +33.3 cm and P = +3 D.

workedExamples.title: Presbyopia: bifocal lens powers
workedExamples.problem: A presbyopic person cannot see clearly beyond 2 m or nearer than 1 m. Find the powers of the two lenses needed in bifocal spectacles.
steps: Step 1: For distant vision, the far point is 2 m, so the distance lens must form the image of an object at infinity at 2 m: f1 = -2 m.
Step 3: For near vision, the object is at 25 cm and the image must be at the near point of 1 m: 1/f2 = 1/(-1) - 1/(-0.25).
Step 5: The upper part of the bifocal lens is the concave distance lens and the lower part is the convex reading lens.

science:electricity.title: Electricity — Student Knowledge Hub for India

outcomes: Define electric current and potential difference with their SI units
State and apply Ohm's law
Calculate resistance from length, area, and resistivity
Analyse series and parallel combinations of resistors
Apply the heating effect of current and electric power formulae
Calculate electrical energy consumption in kWh and its cost
Solve board-style numericals on circuits, power, and energy
Explain and apply Electricity.

concepts.name: Electric Current and Potential Difference
concepts.purpose: Electric current is the rate of flow of electric charge through a conductor, given by I = Q/t. Its SI unit is the ampere (A), where 1 A = 1 coulomb per second. Conventional current flows from the positive terminal to the negative terminal of a cell, while electrons drift in the opposite direction. Potential difference between two points is the work done to move a unit charge from one point to the other, V = W/Q, and its SI unit is the volt (V).

concepts.name: Ohm's Law and Resistance
concepts.purpose: Ohm's law states that the current through a metallic conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it, provided the temperature remains constant. This gives V = IR, where R is the resistance of the conductor. Resistance is the opposition offered by a conductor to the flow of current, and its SI unit is the ohm. A resistor with a straight-line V-I graph through the origin obeys Ohm's law and is called an ohmic conductor.

concepts.name: Factors Affecting Resistance and Resistivity
concepts.purpose: The resistance of a uniform conductor is directly proportional to its length and inversely proportional to its area of cross-section. It also depends on the nature of the material and its temperature. These facts combine into R = rho L / A, where rho is the resistivity of the material. Resistivity is a property of the material itself and its SI unit is the ohm metre; metals have low resistivity while insulators have very high resistivity.

concepts.name: Resistors in Series and Parallel
concepts.purpose: When resistors are joined in series, the same current flows through each of them and the total potential difference is the sum of the individual potential differences. The equivalent resistance is Req = R1 + R2 + R3 + ..., which is greater than the largest individual resistance. When resistors are joined in parallel, the potential difference across each is the same and the total current is the sum of the branch currents. The equivalent resistance is given by 1/Req = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + 1/R3 + ..., which is less than the smallest individual resistance.

concepts.name: Heating Effect of Current and Electric Power
concepts.purpose: When current flows through a resistor, electrical energy is converted into heat because the resistor opposes the flow of charge. The heat produced is H = I^2 R t, which is Joule's law of heating. Electric power is the rate at which electrical energy is consumed, P = VI = I^2 R = V^2 / R. The SI unit of power is the watt (W), and 1 W = 1 joule per second.

concepts.name: Commercial Unit of Electrical Energy and Household Circuits
concepts.purpose: Electrical energy is the product of power and time, E = P x t. For large amounts of energy, the commercial unit is the kilowatt-hour (kWh), where 1 kWh = 3.6 x 10^6 J. One kilowatt-hour is the energy consumed by a 1 kW appliance used for 1 hour, and it is commonly called one unit of electricity. In household wiring, appliances are connected in parallel and each circuit is protected by a fuse or miniature circuit breaker (MCB).

workedExamples.title: Electric current from charge and time
workedExamples.problem: A charge of 60 C flows through a conductor in 1 minute. Find the current.
steps: Step 1: Use I = Q/t.
Step 2: Convert time to seconds: t = 1 minute = 60 s.
Step 3: I = 60 C / 60 s = 1 A.
Step 4: The current through the conductor is 1 ampere.

workedExamples.title: Ohm's law: current through a resistor
workedExamples.problem: A potential difference of 6 V is applied across a resistor of resistance 3 ohm. Find the current through the resistor.
steps: Step 1: Use Ohm's law V = IR.
Step 2: Rearrange to I = V/R.
Step 3: Substitute V = 6 V and R = 3 ohm.
Step 4: I = 6/3 = 2 A.

workedExamples.title: Resistance from resistivity, length, and area
workedExamples.problem: A copper wire of length 2 m and area of cross-section 1 x 10^-6 m^2 has resistivity 1.7 x 10^-8 ohm metre. Find its resistance.
steps: Step 1: Use R = rho L / A.
Step 2: Substitute rho = 1.7 x 10^-8 ohm m, L = 2 m, and A = 1 x 10^-6 m^2.
Step 5: R = 0.034 ohm.

science:magnetic-effects-of-electric-cur.title: Magnetic Effects of Electric Current — Student Knowledge Hub for India

outcomes: Describe a magnetic field and represent it using field lines
Apply the right-hand thumb rule to find the direction of the magnetic field due to a current
Explain the magnetic field of a solenoid and the working of an electromagnet
Use Fleming's left-hand rule to predict the force on a current-carrying conductor
Explain the construction and working of a simple electric motor
Apply electromagnetic induction and Fleming's right-hand rule to generators
Distinguish AC and DC generators and identify their parts
Explain domestic wiring, fuse, earthing, overload, and short circuit safety

concepts.name: Magnetic Field and Magnetic Field Lines
concepts.purpose: A magnetic field is the region around a magnet or a current-carrying conductor in which its magnetic force can be detected. Field lines are drawn from the north pole to the south pole outside a magnet and from south to north inside it, so they form closed loops. The tangent at any point gives the field direction, and closely spaced lines mean a stronger field. Field lines never intersect because a compass needle at a point can point in only one direction.
concepts.realLife: A magnetic compass needle aligns itself along the earth's magnetic field, and a fridge magnet can hold a note because its field acts through a small distance.

concepts.name: Magnetic Field due to a Current-Carrying Conductor
concepts.purpose: Oersted showed that a current-carrying wire deflects a nearby compass needle, so an electric current produces a magnetic field. Around a long straight wire, the field lines are concentric circles in a plane perpendicular to the wire. The right-hand thumb rule gives the direction: point the right thumb along the current, and the curled fingers give the direction of the field lines. The field becomes stronger when the current increases and weaker as the distance from the wire increases.
concepts.realLife: The magnetic field of a current is used in electric bells, relays, loudspeakers, and electromagnetic cranes.

concepts.name: Solenoid and Electromagnet
concepts.purpose: A solenoid is a coil of many circular turns of insulated copper wire wound closely in the shape of a cylinder. When current flows through it, the field inside is uniform and parallel, and the coil behaves like a bar magnet with a north pole at one end and a south pole at the other. Placing a soft iron core inside the solenoid makes an electromagnet, which is magnetic only while current flows. Its strength can be increased by increasing the current, increasing the number of turns, or using a suitable soft iron core.
concepts.realLife: Electromagnets lift scrap iron in cranes, ring electric bells, and operate relays and magnetic locks.

concepts.name: Force on a Current-Carrying Conductor and the Electric Motor
concepts.purpose: A current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field experiences a force because the field of the current interacts with the external field. The force is largest when the conductor is perpendicular to the field and zero when it is parallel to the field. Fleming's left-hand rule gives the direction: the forefinger points along the field, the middle finger along the current, and the thumb gives the force. In a simple DC motor, forces on opposite sides of the coil produce rotation, and a split ring commutator reverses the current every half turn so that rotation continues in the same direction.
concepts.realLife: Electric motors drive fans, washing machines, water pumps, mixers, and electric vehicles.

concepts.name: Electromagnetic Induction, Fleming's Right-Hand Rule and the Generator
concepts.purpose: Faraday discovered that a changing magnetic field through a coil induces an electromotive force and, in a closed circuit, an induced current. This is called electromagnetic induction and can be produced by moving a magnet near a coil, moving a coil near a magnet, or changing the current in a nearby coil. Fleming's right-hand rule gives the direction of the induced current: thumb along motion, forefinger along the field, and middle finger along the induced current. In a generator, a coil rotates in a magnetic field, and the induced current reverses every half rotation, so an AC generator uses slip rings while a DC generator uses a split ring commutator.
concepts.realLife: Power stations use generators driven by steam, water, or wind to supply electricity to homes and industries.

concepts.name: Domestic Electric Circuits, Fuse and Earthing
concepts.purpose: A domestic circuit receives electric power through a live wire and a neutral wire, with a third earth wire for safety. Appliances are connected in parallel so that each gets the full supply voltage and can be switched independently. The fuse is connected in the live wire and contains a thin wire that melts if the current exceeds a safe value, breaking the circuit during overload or short circuit. Earthing connects the metal body of an appliance to the earth, so a leakage current flows safely to the ground instead of through a person.
concepts.realLife: A fuse or MCB protects a home circuit when too many appliances draw current, and earthing protects users of metal-bodied appliances such as refrigerators.

revisionPlan: Read the Magnetic Effects of Electric Current notes and write five key definitions.
Solve three board-style questions and check every step.
Attempt a timed mixed practice set and review mistakes.

workedExamples.title: Field direction around a straight wire
workedExamples.problem: A straight wire carries current vertically upward in the plane of the page. Find the direction of the magnetic field at a point to the right of the wire.
steps: Step 1: Point the right thumb upward along the direction of the current.
Step 2: Curl the fingers of the right hand around the wire.
Step 3: On the right side of the wire, the curled fingers point into the page.
Step 4: Therefore the magnetic field at that point is directed into the page.

workedExamples.title: Poles of a current-carrying solenoid
workedExamples.problem: A solenoid is held horizontally. When viewed from its left end, the current appears to flow anticlockwise. Identify the magnetic polarity of the left end and state two ways to increase the strength of the electromagnet.
steps: Step 1: Use the right-hand rule for a solenoid: curl the fingers in the direction of the current and the thumb points toward the north pole.
Step 2: An anticlockwise current viewed from the left end makes the thumb point toward that end.
Step 3: Therefore the left end acts as the north pole and the right end as the south pole.
Step 4: Increase the current, increase the number of turns, or use a soft iron core to strengthen the electromagnet.

workedExamples.title: Force on a conductor using Fleming's left-hand rule
workedExamples.problem: A straight conductor carries conventional current toward the right of the page. The magnetic field is directed into the page. Find the direction of the force on the conductor.
steps: Step 1: Stretch the forefinger, middle finger, and thumb of the left hand mutually perpendicular.
Step 2: Point the forefinger into the page to represent the magnetic field.

science:our-environment.title: Our Environment — Student Knowledge Hub for India

outcomes: Describe the biotic and abiotic components of an ecosystem
Construct food chains and food webs and identify trophic levels
Apply the 10 percent law to calculate energy transfer between trophic levels
Explain biomagnification and its effect on top consumers
Explain how CFCs deplete the ozone layer and why this matters
Classify wastes as biodegradable or non-biodegradable and choose suitable disposal methods
Explain and apply Our Environment.

concepts.name: Ecosystem and Its Components
concepts.purpose: An ecosystem is a self-regulating unit in which living organisms interact with each other and with their physical environment. The living part is the biotic component and includes producers, consumers and decomposers. The non-living part is the abiotic component and includes sunlight, air, water, soil and temperature. Green plants trap solar energy and make food, consumers eat other organisms, and decomposers break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil.
concepts.realLife: A pond is a complete ecosystem: algae make food, small fish eat them, larger fish eat the small fish, and bacteria in the mud decompose dead plants and animals.

concepts.name: Food Chains, Food Webs and Trophic Levels
concepts.purpose: A food chain shows the step-by-step transfer of food from one organism to another, beginning with a producer. Each step in the chain is a trophic level: producers form the first level, herbivores the second, and carnivores the third and higher levels. In nature, food chains do not exist alone; they interconnect to form a food web, which makes the ecosystem more stable. Decomposers act on dead organisms at every level and return nutrients to the environment.
concepts.realLife: In a field, grass is eaten by grasshoppers, grasshoppers by frogs, frogs by snakes and snakes by hawks; the same grass may also be eaten by rabbits, which are eaten by hawks, forming a food web.

concepts.name: Energy Flow and the 10 Percent Law
concepts.purpose: Energy enters an ecosystem as sunlight and is trapped by producers during photosynthesis. It then passes to consumers, but at each trophic level most of the energy is used in respiration, lost as heat or left in undigested material. The 10 percent law states that only about 10 percent of the energy at one trophic level is transferred to the next level. Because so much energy is lost, food chains are usually short, with only four or five trophic levels.
concepts.realLife: A large area of grass can support only a few hawks because most of the energy is lost at each step from grass to insects to frogs to snakes to hawks.

concepts.name: Biomagnification of Harmful Substances
concepts.purpose: Biomagnification is the increase in concentration of a harmful, non-biodegradable substance as it passes from one trophic level to the next. Pesticides, heavy metals and some industrial chemicals are not broken down by organisms and are not easily excreted. They accumulate in the bodies of organisms, so each higher trophic level receives and retains a larger dose. Humans and other top consumers are therefore at the greatest risk.
concepts.realLife: A pesticide sprayed on a field may be present in very low concentration in water, but it becomes concentrated in fish and then in the birds or people that eat the fish.

concepts.name: Ozone Layer and Its Depletion
concepts.purpose: The ozone layer is a region of the stratosphere rich in ozone (O3) that absorbs most of the harmful ultraviolet radiation from the Sun. Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs), used in refrigerators and aerosol sprays, rise into the stratosphere where ultraviolet light breaks them down and releases chlorine atoms. Each chlorine atom can destroy many ozone molecules in a chain reaction, thinning the ozone layer. Greater ultraviolet radiation reaching the Earth increases the risk of skin cancer and eye damage and harms plants and aquatic life.
concepts.realLife: Older refrigerators and air conditioners used CFCs; replacing them with ozone-friendly refrigerants helps protect the ozone layer.

concepts.name: Biodegradable and Non-biodegradable Waste
concepts.purpose: Biodegradable wastes, such as food scraps, paper and cotton, are broken down by microorganisms and can be composted. Non-biodegradable wastes, such as plastic, glass, metals and many chemicals, are not broken down by microorganisms and persist in the environment for a long time. Good waste management means reducing waste at source, segregating it, reusing and recycling materials, composting biodegradable waste and sending hazardous waste for safe disposal. Poor disposal pollutes soil, water and air and harms wildlife.
concepts.realLife: A household can compost vegetable peels, recycle paper and metal, reuse cloth bags and keep batteries and medicines out of ordinary bins.

mindMap.title: Our Environment - Mind Map

keyPoints: Food Chains, Food Webs and Trophic Levels
Energy Flow and the 10 Percent Law
misconceptions: Decomposers are a type of consumer that eats dead animals - FALSE: decomposers break down dead matter and recycle nutrients; they are not consumers in the food-chain sense.
Energy is recycled in an ecosystem just like nutrients - FALSE: nutrients cycle, but energy flows one way and is lost as heat.
A food chain and a food web are the same thing - FALSE: a food web is made of several interconnected food chains.
Biomagnification means the total amount of pollutant in the ecosystem increases - FALSE: it means the concentration in organisms increases at higher trophic levels.
The ozone hole is the same as global warming - FALSE: ozone depletion concerns ultraviolet radiation; global warming concerns heat-trapping gases.
Ozone is harmful everywhere and should be removed from the atmosphere - FALSE: stratospheric ozone protects life; ground-level ozone is a pollutant.

quickCheck.question: Which of these is a biotic component of an ecosystem?
quickCheck.explanation: Grass is a living organism, so it is a biotic component.

quickCheck.question: Which organism is a producer?
quickCheck.explanation: A green plant makes its own food by photosynthesis, so it is a producer.

quickCheck.question: A herbivore is a:
quickCheck.explanation: A herbivore eats producers and is therefore a primary consumer.

quickCheck.question: Bacteria and fungi that break down dead matter are called:
quickCheck.explanation: Bacteria and fungi are decomposers that break down dead organic matter.

workedExamples.title: Identifying trophic levels in a food chain
workedExamples.problem: Consider the food chain: grass, grasshopper, frog, snake, hawk. Identify the producer, the consumers and the trophic level of each organism. What would happen if all the frogs were removed?
steps: Step 1: Identify the producer. Grass makes its own food by photosynthesis, so it is the producer.
Step 2: Identify the consumers. Grasshopper, frog, snake and hawk cannot make their own food, so they are consumers.
Step 3: Assign trophic levels. Grass is the first trophic level; grasshopper is the second; frog is the third; snake is the fourth; hawk is the fifth.
Step 4: Classify consumers by diet. Grasshopper is a primary consumer (herbivore), frog and snake are carnivores, and hawk is the top carnivore.
Step 5: Predict the effect of removing frogs. Grasshoppers would initially increase because their predator is gone.
Step 6: More grasshoppers would eat more grass, so the grass population would decline.
Step 7: Snakes would lose a food source and their numbers would fall or they would shift to other prey.
Step 8: The whole chain would be disturbed, showing that organisms in a food chain are interdependent.

workedExamples.title: Applying the 10 percent law
workedExamples.problem: In a food chain, the producers capture 10,000 J of energy from sunlight. Using the 10 percent law, calculate the energy available to the primary consumer, the secondary consumer and the tertiary consumer.
steps: Step 1: Write the 10 percent law: only about 10 percent of the energy at one trophic level passes to the next.
Step 2: Energy at the producer level = 10,000 J.
Step 3: Energy available to the primary consumer = 10 percent of 10,000 J = 1,000 J.
Step 4: Energy available to the secondary consumer = 10 percent of 1,000 J = 100 J.
Step 5: Energy available to the tertiary consumer = 10 percent of 100 J = 10 J.
Step 6: Check the pattern: the energy falls by a factor of 10 at each step.
Step 7: Explain the consequence: most energy is lost as heat and in life processes, so top consumers receive very little energy.

workedExamples.title: Why biomagnification harms top consumers
workedExamples.problem: A pesticide is present in very low concentration in a pond. Explain why a fish-eating bird may contain a much higher concentration of the pesticide than the water, and why this is a health concern.
steps: Step 1: The pesticide is non-biodegradable, so microorganisms cannot break it down.
Step 2: It is taken up by tiny aquatic plants and animals, where it accumulates in their bodies.
Step 3: Small fish eat many of these organisms and retain the pesticide from each meal.
Step 4: Larger fish eat many small fish, so the pesticide concentration increases again.
Step 5: The fish-eating bird eats many large fish and therefore receives a large cumulative dose.
Step 6: At each trophic level the substance is not excreted efficiently, so its concentration rises; this is biomagnification.
Step 7: High concentrations can damage the nervous system, reproduction and development of top consumers, including humans.
Step 8: Reducing pesticide use and preventing runoff into water bodies lowers the risk.

tips: Write the given information and what is asked before solving.
Show every step; board marking rewards reasoning.
Reattempt wrong questions after 24 hours.

science:management-of-natural-resources.title: Management of Natural Resources — Student Knowledge Hub for India

outcomes: Explain sustainable management of renewable and non-renewable natural resources
Describe forest and wildlife resources and identify the stakeholders involved
Explain the Chipko movement and Joint Forest Management as examples of people's participation
Evaluate the benefits and costs of dams and describe rainwater harvesting and watershed management
Explain why coal and petroleum must be conserved and how their use causes pollution
Apply the three Rs and sustainable practices to everyday resource decisions
Explain and apply Management of Natural Resources.

concepts.name: Natural Resources and Sustainable Management
concepts.purpose: Natural resources are the materials and energy obtained from nature that support life and economic activity. Renewable resources, such as sunlight, wind and forests, can be replenished, while non-renewable resources, such as coal and petroleum, are formed over very long periods and are exhausted by use. Sustainable management means using resources so that present needs are met without damaging the environment or reducing what is available to future generations. The three Rs, reduce, reuse and recycle, are practical steps toward sustainability.
concepts.realLife: Carrying a cloth bag, repairing appliances and sorting waste for recycling all reduce the demand for new raw materials.

concepts.name: Forests, Wildlife and Biodiversity
concepts.purpose: Forests provide timber, fuel, fodder, food, medicines and clean water, and they protect soil and regulate the climate. They are also habitats for a large part of the world's biodiversity, the variety of plants, animals and microorganisms. Wildlife conservation protects species and their habitats so that ecosystems remain stable. Forests have several stakeholders, including local communities, the forest department, industrialists and conservationists, whose interests must be balanced.
concepts.realLife: A village near a forest may depend on it for firewood and fodder, while a timber company wants logs and a conservation group wants the habitat protected, so management must balance these claims.

concepts.name: Chipko Movement and Joint Forest Management
concepts.purpose: The Chipko movement began in the 1970s in the Garhwal Himalayas, in present-day Uttarakhand, when local people, especially women, hugged trees to prevent contractors from cutting them. It showed that communities who depend on forests have a strong interest in protecting them. Joint Forest Management, introduced in the 1980s, brought the forest department and local communities together through village forest committees. Communities help protect and regenerate degraded forests and receive a share of forest products and benefits.
concepts.realLife: Village forest committees protect newly planted areas from grazing and fire, and in return they can collect agreed quantities of fodder, fuelwood and other products.

concepts.name: Water Resources, Dams and Rainwater Harvesting
concepts.purpose: Fresh water is a limited resource and must be managed carefully. Dams store river water and supply it for irrigation, drinking and industry, and they can generate hydroelectricity and help control floods. However, dams also submerge land, displace people, disturb river ecosystems, trap silt and can cause waterlogging and salinity. Rainwater harvesting collects and stores rainwater from roofs or catchments, and watershed management conserves water and soil across a whole drainage area. These methods recharge groundwater and reduce dependence on distant water sources.
concepts.realLife: A rooftop rainwater harvesting system can store water for gardening and recharge a borewell, reducing pressure on municipal supply.

concepts.name: Coal, Petroleum and the Need for Conservation
concepts.purpose: Coal and petroleum are fossil fuels formed from the remains of living organisms buried over millions of years. They are non-renewable because the rate at which we use them is far greater than the rate at which they form. Burning them releases carbon dioxide, sulphur dioxide, nitrogen oxides and particulate matter, which pollute the air and contribute to climate change and acid rain. Conserving fossil fuels means improving efficiency, reducing waste and shifting to cleaner alternatives such as solar and wind energy.
concepts.realLife: Using a bus or metro instead of a private car for a daily commute reduces petrol consumption and air pollution per person.

concepts.name: Conservation, Equity and People's Participation
concepts.purpose: Conservation is the protection and careful use of natural resources so that they last. It is not only a government task: local communities, industry, scientists, non-governmental organisations and individual citizens all have roles. Sustainable management must also be fair, because people who depend directly on forests, water and land should share in the benefits and be involved in decisions. Long-term planning, public awareness and pollution control are essential parts of conservation.
concepts.realLife: A city can involve residents in waste segregation, protect a local lake with community groups and require industries to treat wastewater before discharge.

mindMap.title: Management of Natural Resources - Mind Map

keyPoints: Chipko Movement and Joint Forest Management
Water Resources, Dams and Rainwater Harvesting
Coal, Petroleum and the Need for Conservation
misconceptions: Conservation means never using a natural resource - FALSE: conservation means careful, sustainable use, not total non-use.
Renewable resources cannot be depleted - FALSE: renewable resources can be exhausted or damaged if they are used faster than they regenerate.
All fossil fuels will last for centuries, so there is no need to conserve them - FALSE: fossil fuels are finite and are consumed far faster than they form.
Dams have only benefits - FALSE: dams also cause submergence, displacement, silting and ecological damage.
The Chipko movement was only about planting trees - FALSE: it was a protest against commercial felling, in which people hugged trees to stop them being cut.
Joint Forest Management gives forests entirely to local communities - FALSE: it is a partnership between communities and the forest department.

quickCheck.question: Which of these is a non-renewable resource?

quickCheck.question: Which of these is a fossil fuel?

quickCheck.explanation: The three Rs are Reduce, Reuse and Recycle.

workedExamples.title: Evaluating the benefits and costs of a dam
workedExamples.problem: A dam is proposed across a river to supply irrigation water and electricity. List two benefits and two costs of the project, and state what information is needed before a decision is taken.
steps: Step 1: Identify the benefits. The dam can store water for irrigation and supply drinking water.
Step 2: A second benefit is hydroelectricity generation, and the reservoir can help moderate floods.
Step 3: Identify the costs. Large areas of land may be submerged, including forests and farmland.
Step 4: People living in the submerged area may be displaced and lose their livelihoods.
Step 5: The dam can trap silt, alter the river's flow and damage aquatic habitats and fish migration.
Step 6: Information needed includes the number of people affected, the ecological value of the submerged area, the cost of rehabilitation and the expected benefits.
Step 7: A decision should compare alternatives such as smaller dams, rainwater harvesting or watershed management.
Step 8: The best choice balances development with social justice and environmental protection.

workedExamples.title: Calculating rainwater harvested from a roof
workedExamples.problem: A school has a flat roof of area 100 square metres. During a spell of rain, 50 mm of rainfall is recorded. If the harvesting system can collect 80 percent of the rain falling on the roof, calculate the volume of water collected in litres.
steps: Step 1: Convert rainfall to metres: 50 mm = 50/1000 m = 0.05 m.
Step 2: Volume of rain falling on the roof = roof area x rainfall depth = 100 m2 x 0.05 m = 5 m3.
Step 3: The system collects 80 percent of this volume, so collected volume = 5 x 0.80 = 4 m3.
Step 4: Convert cubic metres to litres using 1 m3 = 1000 L.
Step 5: Collected water = 4 x 1000 = 4000 L.
Step 6: Check the calculation: 100 x 0.05 = 5; 5 x 0.8 = 4; 4 x 1000 = 4000.
Step 7: The harvested water can be stored or used to recharge groundwater.

workedExamples.title: How people's participation protects forests
workedExamples.problem: Explain how the Chipko movement and Joint Forest Management show the importance of involving local communities in forest protection.
steps: Step 1: Local communities depend on forests for fuelwood, fodder, food and water, so they have a direct interest in the forest's survival.
Step 2: In the Chipko movement, people hugged trees to stop contractors from felling them.
Step 3: The movement showed that forest protection succeeds when the people who live near the forest are involved and benefit from it.
Step 4: Joint Forest Management creates village forest committees in partnership with the forest department.
Step 5: Communities help protect and regenerate degraded forest land and receive a share of forest products.
Step 6: This partnership reduces conflict and gives people a long-term stake in conservation.
Step 7: Participation also brings local knowledge about species, water sources and traditional practices.
Step 8: Therefore sustainable forest management combines government regulation with community responsibility.

concepts.name: The French Revolution and the Idea of the Nation
concepts.purpose: The French Revolution gave nationalism its modern political meaning: the nation is not the king but the people, and the people share laws, symbols, language, and a common future.
concepts.realLife: Modern states still use flags, anthems, common laws, and a shared language to build a sense of belonging among citizens.

concepts.name: Liberalism, Nationalism, and Economic Change
concepts.purpose: Liberalism supplied the economic and legal programme that often travelled with nationalism, and the Zollverein showed how economic unity can prepare the ground for political unity.
concepts.realLife: Customs unions and common markets, such as the European Union, follow the same logic as the Zollverein: remove internal barriers to increase trade.

concepts.name: Conservatism and the Congress of Vienna
concepts.purpose: The Congress tried to undo the French Revolution and prevent another one by restoring monarchies and balancing power among the great states.
concepts.realLife: Peace conferences still redraw borders and create buffer zones or alliances to prevent future conflict.

concepts.name: The Revolutions of 1830 and 1848
concepts.purpose: The revolutions show the strength of liberal and nationalist demands, and also their limits when rulers retained control of the army and when liberals feared popular democracy.
concepts.realLife: Food prices, unemployment, and exclusion from political power remain common triggers of protest and political change.

concepts.name: The Unification of Germany and Italy
concepts.purpose: The two unifications show that nationalism could be achieved by war and statecraft as well as by popular movements, and that the two paths produced different political systems.
concepts.realLife: Modern state-building still combines diplomacy, military power, and popular identity, and the German model shaped later ideas of national unity.

concepts.name: Britain, the Balkans, and Aggressive Nationalism
concepts.purpose: The British case shows that nation-states can be built gradually through parliament and union, while the Balkans shows how nationalism can become entangled with great-power rivalry and war.
concepts.realLife: Debates about Scottish independence, Irish unity, and language identity show that union and nationhood remain live political questions.

Analyse the programme, spread, and withdrawal of the Non-Cooperation Movement

concepts.name: The First World War, the Rowlatt Act, and Jallianwala Bagh
concepts.purpose: This phase explains why moderate constitutional politics gave way to mass protest and why Gandhi became the central leader of the national movement.
concepts.realLife: Understanding how war expenditure, inflation, and emergency laws can turn ordinary economic hardship into political resistance.

concepts.name: Satyagraha and the Non-Cooperation Movement
concepts.purpose: Non-Cooperation was the first nationwide mass movement led by the Congress, and it revealed both the power and the limits of non-violent mass politics.
concepts.realLife: Boycotts and non-violent resistance are still used by citizens and consumer groups to press for change.

concepts.name: Civil Disobedience and the Salt March
concepts.purpose: Civil Disobedience turned nationalist politics into a direct challenge to colonial law and made the Congress a mass organisation with a national programme.
concepts.realLife: Symbolic acts of law-breaking, such as peaceful sit-ins, show how a single issue can expose the wider unfairness of a system.

concepts.name: The Quit India Movement
concepts.purpose: Quit India marked the end of the Congress's willingness to negotiate within the colonial system and made immediate independence the central demand.
concepts.realLife: Understanding how a movement can continue through local initiative when its leaders are arrested.

concepts.name: The Muslim League and the Demand for Pakistan
concepts.purpose: The rise of the Muslim League explains how religious identity became a basis for a separate state and why a negotiated united India became impossible.
concepts.realLife: Understanding how political organisations use identity, representation, and fear to build support in divided societies.

concepts.name: Partition and Independence in 1947
concepts.purpose: Partition shows that independence came with a territorial and human cost, and that the national movement's goal of unity was not achieved.
concepts.realLife: Understanding how borders and migration continue to affect citizenship, identity, and regional politics in South Asia.

concepts.name: Silk Routes, Trade, and Cultural Exchange
concepts.purpose: The silk routes show that long-distance trade and cultural exchange existed long before modern globalisation.
concepts.realLife: Modern trade corridors and shipping lanes still connect distant markets and carry both goods and ideas.

concepts.name: The Columbian Exchange and the Conquest of the Americas
concepts.purpose: The Columbian exchange explains how the modern global food system, plantation economy, and Atlantic slave trade were created.
concepts.realLife: The potato, tomato, chilli, and maize in Indian food are all results of the Columbian exchange.

concepts.name: Colonialism, Indian Trade, and the Global Economy
concepts.purpose: Colonialism reshaped global trade so that colonies supplied raw materials and markets while industrial powers captured most of the value.
concepts.realLife: Debates about unequal trade, raw material exports, and protection of local industry still echo the colonial pattern.

concepts.name: Indentured Labour and Global Migration
concepts.purpose: Indentured labour shows how abolition did not end coerced labour and how migration created new multicultural societies.
concepts.realLife: Indian diaspora communities in Mauritius, Fiji, Trinidad, and Guyana trace their origins to indentured migration.

concepts.name: The Great Depression
concepts.purpose: The Great Depression shows how closely national economies are connected and how a financial crisis in one country can become a global slump.
concepts.realLife: The 2008 financial crisis and the COVID-19 recession show similar patterns of job losses and government intervention.

concepts.name: Bretton Woods, Decolonisation, and Modern Globalisation
concepts.purpose: Bretton Woods created the institutions and rules that shaped the post-war world economy and prepared the ground for modern globalisation.
concepts.realLife: IMF loans during balance-of-payments crises and World Bank development projects still affect countries today.

concepts.name: Proto-industrialisation and Merchant Capital
concepts.purpose: It explains why industrial production first grew outside guild-controlled towns and how merchant capital prepared the ground for the factory system.
concepts.realLife: A modern garment brand that gives cloth to home-based tailors, controls the design, and sells the finished clothes under its own label works in a similar way.

concepts.name: The Factory System and Cotton
concepts.purpose: It shows how production moved from scattered homes to centralised workplaces and why cotton became the engine of early industrial capitalism.
concepts.realLife: A modern garment export unit that combines cutting, stitching and quality checks under one roof still follows the logic of the factory system.

concepts.name: Steam, Coal, Iron and Railways
concepts.purpose: It explains the energy and transport revolution that made large-scale industry possible and linked factories to distant markets.
concepts.realLife: Electricity grids, freight corridors and container ports play the same linking role today that steam power and railways played in the nineteenth century.

concepts.name: Manchester and the Human Cost of Industrialisation
concepts.purpose: It balances the story of growth with the social costs of industrial capitalism and introduces the debate on labour rights.
concepts.realLife: Debates about factory safety, working hours and child labour in global supply chains echo the Manchester experience.

concepts.name: Indian Textiles, the East India Company and Deindustrialisation
concepts.purpose: It explains how colonial power reshaped Indian production and why the Indian textile industry declined while British industry grew.
concepts.realLife: It helps interpret how trade rules, tariffs and unequal power affect artisans and small producers today.

concepts.name: Indian Industrialists, Advertisements and Nationalism
concepts.purpose: It shows that industrialisation in India was not only colonial exploitation; Indian capital and advertising actively shaped markets and political consciousness.
concepts.realLife: Branding, packaging and Made in India campaigns are descendants of nineteenth-century labels and swadeshi advertising.

quickCheck.question: Proto-industrialisation refers to:

Trade carried out only by guilds in towns

workedExamples.title: Why merchants moved cloth production to the countryside
workedExamples.problem: Explain why merchants in eighteenth-century Europe moved cloth production to the countryside instead of expanding it in towns.
steps: Step 1: Town guilds controlled entry into a trade, fixed prices and limited competition.
Step 2: A merchant who wanted to expand output could not easily hire more workers or open new workshops in a guild town.
Step 3: Rural households were willing to work for low payments because many peasants had small plots and needed extra income.
Step 4: The merchant supplied raw material and sometimes advances, collected the finished cloth and sold it in distant markets.
Step 5: This domestic system, or proto-industrialisation, gave the merchant control over production without owning a factory.

workedExamples.title: How the factory system reorganised production
workedExamples.problem: How did the factory system change the organisation of production in Britain?
steps: Step 1: Production moved from scattered households into large buildings owned by capitalists.
Step 2: Machines such as the spinning jenny, water frame and mule increased output per worker.
Step 3: Workers were hired for wages and had to follow fixed hours, rules and supervision.
Step 4: Owners controlled raw material, tools, credit and the sale of finished goods.
Step 5: Costs fell and output rose, but workers lost the independence they had in household production.

workedExamples.title: Steam, coal, iron and railways
workedExamples.problem: Explain the role of steam power, coal, iron and railways in the industrial revolution.
steps: Step 1: James Watt's improved steam engine converted coal into steady power for mines, mills and transport.
Step 2: Coal was abundant and became the main fuel, while coke helped produce cheaper and stronger iron.
Step 3: Iron was used for machines, rails, bridges and ships, linking mining, metalwork and transport.
Step 4: Railways from the 1830s carried coal, cotton and finished goods faster and at lower cost.
Step 5: Faster transport widened markets and encouraged factories to produce on a larger scale.

Show every step; board marking rewards reasoning.

concepts.name: Manuscript Culture and the First Printed Books in East Asia
concepts.purpose: It shows that print did not appear from nowhere; it grew out of older manuscript practices and East Asian technologies.
concepts.realLife: A handwritten family recipe book shared among relatives is closer to manuscript culture, while a printed cookbook sold in shops belongs to print culture.

concepts.name: Gutenberg and the Printing Press
concepts.purpose: It explains the technical breakthrough that made cheap, rapid and multiple copies of a text possible in Europe.
concepts.realLife: A modern printing press still uses the same basic idea: a reusable master image, ink and pressure on paper, though the technology is now digital.

concepts.name: The Print Revolution and the Reading Public
concepts.purpose: It explains how print changed the relationship between people, knowledge and public debate.
concepts.realLife: The shift from a few expensive textbooks to cheap books, newspapers and online articles follows a similar pattern of widening access.

concepts.name: Religion, Enlightenment and Censorship
concepts.purpose: It shows print as a contested power: the same technology could spread reform, science, dissent and state control.
concepts.realLife: Debates over internet censorship, banned books and fake news show that control over information is still a political struggle.

concepts.name: Print Comes to India
concepts.purpose: It explains how a technology introduced by missionaries and colonial officials became a tool for Indian writers, reformers and nationalists.
concepts.realLife: Regional-language newspapers and publishing houses continue the tradition of print in Indian public life.

concepts.name: Print, Reform, Women and Nationalism
concepts.purpose: It shows how print helped create a public sphere in India in which reform, women's voices and nationalism could be debated.
concepts.realLife: Blogs, social-media campaigns and independent news sites today perform a similar role of allowing new voices to enter public debate.

quickCheck.question: The earliest kind of print technology developed in:
quickCheck.explanation: Hand printing with woodblocks first developed in East Asia.

quickCheck.question: Woodblock printing involves:

quickCheck.explanation: A carved and inked wooden block transfers its image to paper under pressure.

quickCheck.question: Gutenberg's first major printed book was the:
quickCheck.explanation: Gutenberg printed the Bible in the 1450s using movable metal type.

quickCheck.question: Movable type means:
options: Individual letters that can be arranged and reused
A whole page carved on one block
quickCheck.explanation: Movable type consists of separate pieces of type that can be rearranged for different pages.

workedExamples.title: Development of print in China and Japan
workedExamples.problem: Describe how printing developed in China and Japan before it reached Europe.
steps: Step 1: China, Japan and Korea developed hand printing using woodblocks.
Step 2: From AD 594 books in China were printed by rubbing paper against inked woodblocks.
Step 3: Chinese books were folded in an accordion shape, which suited woodblock printing.
Step 4: Buddhist missionaries carried printing to Japan, where monasteries printed religious texts.
Step 5: Japanese printers also produced ukiyo-e pictures of city life, actors and landscapes for a popular market.

workedExamples.title: Gutenberg's technical contribution
workedExamples.problem: Explain the main features of Gutenberg's printing press and why it was revolutionary.
steps: Step 1: Gutenberg used movable metal type instead of carving a whole page on wood.
Step 2: Lead moulds allowed identical letters to be cast and reused in different combinations.
Step 3: He adapted the olive press to apply even pressure to inked type and paper.
Step 4: The system could produce many copies of a book quickly and at lower cost.
Step 5: His Bible, printed in the 1450s, proved that the new technology could produce fine books.

workedExamples.title: Print, Reformation and Enlightenment
workedExamples.problem: How did print contribute to the Protestant Reformation and the Enlightenment?
steps: Step 1: Print allowed reformers to circulate arguments quickly to many readers.
Step 2: Luther's Ninety Five Theses of 1517 were printed and spread across Europe.
Step 3: Printed pamphlets and Bibles weakened the Church's monopoly over religious knowledge.
Step 4: Enlightenment writers used print to spread ideas of reason, science and individual rights.
Step 5: Authorities responded with censorship, but print made it difficult to suppress new ideas completely.

social-science:resources-and-development.title: Resources and Development — Student Knowledge Hub for India

outcomes: Explain development as a combination of income and non-income goals
Distinguish national income from per capita income
Calculate per capita income and interpret its limitations
Describe the three dimensions of the Human Development Index
Explain why public facilities are essential for human development
Define sustainable development and identify threats to sustainability
Compare development outcomes using income, health, and education
Solve board-style case and data questions on development indicators

concepts.name: Meaning of Development
concepts.purpose: The concept widens development from economic growth to human welfare. It explains why governments, communities, and individuals often disagree about what counts as progress.
concepts.realLife: A new highway may reduce travel time for commuters but displace families living along the route, so the same project creates benefits for some and losses for others.

concepts.name: Income and Other Goals
concepts.purpose: This concept explains why income alone is an incomplete measure and why policy must address working conditions, public services, and social justice.
concepts.realLife: A high salary cannot compensate for toxic air, unsafe transport, or a lack of schools for children; people often trade income for a better quality of life.

concepts.name: Per Capita Income and Its Limits
concepts.purpose: The concept teaches how averages are calculated and why they can mislead. It prepares students to interpret development data critically.
concepts.realLife: Two colonies can have the same average income, but in one the income is shared evenly while in the other a single rich household dominates the average.

concepts.name: Human Development Index
concepts.purpose: HDI provides a broader comparison of development than income alone. It shows that a country can have modest income but good health and education, or high income but poor human outcomes.
concepts.realLife: A country with lower average income but widespread schooling and health care can rank higher on human development than a richer country with unequal access.

concepts.name: Public Facilities and Human Development
concepts.purpose: The concept explains why governments provide essential services and why public spending on health and education is a development investment, not just welfare.
concepts.realLife: A public health centre, a government school, and a municipal water supply can improve life chances even when private incomes are low.

concepts.name: Sustainable Development
concepts.purpose: The concept links development to resource limits and intergenerational justice. It explains why short-term growth can destroy the resource base on which future development depends.
concepts.realLife: If a city extracts more groundwater than rain recharges, the water table falls and future residents face shortages, even if current residents enjoy abundant supply.

mindMap.title: Development - Mind Map

keyPoints: Per Capita Income and Its Limits
misconceptions: Development means only higher income - FALSE: health, education, dignity, equality, and freedom are also goals.
A higher average income means everyone is better off - FALSE: the average can hide severe inequality.
HDI uses only income - FALSE: HDI combines health, education, and income.
Economic growth and development are the same - FALSE: growth can occur without improvements in well-being.
All development goals agree with one another - FALSE: projects can benefit some people and harm others.
Sustainable development means stopping growth - FALSE: it means meeting needs without destroying the resource base for the future.

quickCheck.question: Development means:
quickCheck.explanation: Development includes income and non-income improvements in people's lives.

quickCheck.question: Per capita income is:
quickCheck.explanation: It divides total national income by the number of people.

quickCheck.question: Which is a non-income goal of development?
quickCheck.explanation: Dignity and equality are social goals beyond income.

quickCheck.question: HDI measures development using:
quickCheck.explanation: HDI combines life expectancy, schooling, and per capita income.

revisionPlan: Read the Resources and Development notes and write five key definitions.
Solve three board-style questions and check every step.
Attempt a timed mixed practice set and review mistakes.

workedExamples.title: Calculating Per Capita Income
workedExamples.problem: A country has a national income of Rs 80,000 crore and a population of 4 crore. Calculate its per capita income. If another country has a national income of Rs 60,000 crore and a population of 2 crore, which has the higher per capita income?

workedExamples.title: How an Average Hides Inequality
workedExamples.problem: Country A has four citizens with annual incomes of Rs 10,000 each. Country B has four citizens with incomes of Rs 2,000, Rs 2,000, Rs 2,000, and Rs 34,000. Both have the same average income. Explain what the average hides.

workedExamples.title: Comparing Human Development
workedExamples.problem: Country X has life expectancy of 70 years, average schooling of 8 years, and per capita income of $5,000. Country Y has life expectancy of 60 years, average schooling of 5 years, and per capita income of $8,000. Which country is likely to have higher human development, and why?
