social-science:consumer-rights.title: Consumer Rights — Student Knowledge Hub for India

outcomes: Explain who a consumer is and how consumers can be exploited
Describe the six consumer rights with examples
Explain the responsibilities that accompany consumer rights
Outline the main features of COPRA and the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
Describe the three-tier consumer court system and the redressal process
Identify standardisation marks and explain their role in quality assurance
Analyse case studies on defective goods, overcharging, and misleading advertisements
Solve board-style questions on consumer protection and redressal

concepts.name: Consumers and Consumer Exploitation
concepts.purpose: The concept explains why consumers need legal protection and how everyday market transactions can cause harm.
concepts.realLife: Buying a packet of food that is past its expiry date, or paying more than the printed MRP, are common forms of consumer exploitation.

concepts.name: Consumer Rights
concepts.purpose: The concept gives a framework for identifying which right is violated in a given case and what remedy is available.
concepts.realLife: A defective pressure cooker, a hidden charge on a bill, or a refused refund can each violate a different consumer right.

concepts.name: Consumer Responsibilities
concepts.purpose: The concept balances rights with duties and explains how consumer action makes legal protection effective.
concepts.realLife: A consumer who keeps the bill and complains within time can get a replacement, while one who discards the bill may be unable to prove the purchase.

concepts.name: COPRA and the Consumer Protection Act
concepts.purpose: The concept explains the legal foundation of consumer protection and how the law has adapted to new markets such as online shopping.
concepts.realLife: A consumer who buys a defective product online can use the same consumer protection framework as a buyer in a physical shop.

concepts.name: Consumer Courts and Redressal
concepts.purpose: The concept explains the practical route to redressal and the importance of time limits and evidence.
concepts.realLife: A consumer with a defective washing machine can file a complaint with the appropriate commission, attach the bill and warranty, and seek repair or replacement.

concepts.name: Standardisation Marks and Quality Assurance
concepts.purpose: The concept explains how quality certification reduces information problems and helps consumers make safer choices.
concepts.realLife: An electric iron with the ISI mark, a jar of honey with AGMARK, hallmarked gold jewellery, and packaged food with the FSSAI mark carry different quality assurances.

mindMap.title: Consumer Rights - Mind Map

keyPoints: COPRA and the Consumer Protection Act
misconceptions: A consumer is anyone who buys goods for resale - FALSE: a consumer buys for personal use, not resale or production.
Consumer rights apply only to expensive goods - FALSE: they apply to goods and services across price ranges.
MRP is a minimum price - FALSE: MRP is the maximum retail price, and charging above it is unfair.
The ISI mark guarantees perfect quality - FALSE: it certifies compliance with specified standards, not perfection.
Consumer courts are only for rich people - FALSE: the law provides accessible redressal, including mediation and online filing.
A complaint can be filed at any time - FALSE: generally it must be filed within two years of the cause of action.

quickCheck.question: A consumer is a person who:
quickCheck.explanation: A consumer buys goods or services for personal use, not resale.

quickCheck.question: Which right protects consumers from hazardous goods?
quickCheck.explanation: The right to safety protects life and health from dangerous products.

quickCheck.question: MRP stands for:
quickCheck.explanation: MRP is the maximum price at which a product may be sold to the consumer.

quickCheck.question: The ISI mark is used mainly for:
quickCheck.explanation: ISI certifies many industrial and electrical products under BIS.

revisionPlan: Read the Consumer Rights notes and write five key definitions.
Solve three board-style questions and check every step.
Attempt a timed mixed practice set and review mistakes.

workedExamples.problem: A consumer buys a new smartphone. The battery overheats within a week, the seller refuses to replace it, and the advertisement had claimed a battery life that the phone does not deliver. Identify the consumer rights that are affected and the remedy available.

workedExamples.title: Overcharging Above MRP
workedExamples.problem: A shop sells a product with a printed MRP of Rs 1,200 for Rs 1,350. Calculate the excess charged and the percentage overcharge.

workedExamples.title: Expired Food and the Limitation Period
workedExamples.problem: A consumer buys packaged food on 10 January 2025. The packet shows an expiry date of 31 December 2024. The consumer falls ill after eating it. Explain the rights violated, the evidence needed, and the deadline for filing a complaint.

Show every step; board marking rewards reasoning.
Reattempt wrong questions after 24 hours.

outcomes: Modals are helping verbs that express ability, possibility, permission, obligation, advice or certainty.

keyPoints: Each, every, either, neither, everyone, somebody = singular.

With 'either...or' and 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject.

english:first-flight-poetry.summary: Literature Textbook & Supplementary Reading · Literature Textbook & Supplementary Reading

outcomes: First Flight poetry includes Dust of Snow, Fire and Ice, A Tiger in the Zoo, How to Tell Wild Animals, The Ball Poem, Amanda!, The Trees, Fog, The Tale of Custard the Dragon and For Anne Gregory.
Poetry questions test central idea, poetic devices, tone and message.
Explain the device and its effect, not only its name.
Explain and apply First Flight - Poetry.

concepts.name: First Flight - Poetry
concepts.purpose: Build clear understanding of First Flight - Poetry with definitions, examples and exam-style practice.

items.title: Poem map: title -> speaker -> situation -> images -> tone -> theme.
Device cards: metaphor, simile, personification, alliteration, repetition, irony.

keyPoints: Dust of Snow: small moments can change a mood.
Fire and Ice: desire and hatred as forces of destruction.
A Tiger in the Zoo: freedom versus captivity.
The Trees: nature's slow reclaiming of space.

quickCheck.question: What does the tiger in 'A Tiger in the Zoo' represent?
quickCheck.explanation: The poem contrasts the tiger's natural freedom with its zoo cage.

revisionPlan: Write the central idea of each poem in two lines.
List two poetic devices per poem with examples.
Practise extract-based questions.
Read the First Flight - Poetry notes and write five key definitions.
Solve three board-style questions and check every step.
Attempt a timed mixed practice set and review mistakes.

tips: Identify the speaker and the situation.
Quote the image and explain its effect.
Link the device to the theme.
Write the given information and what is asked before solving.
Show every step; board marking rewards reasoning.
Reattempt wrong questions after 24 hours.

english:footprints-without-feet-suppleme.summary: Literature Textbook & Supplementary Reading · Literature Textbook & Supplementary Reading

outcomes: Footprints without Feet includes A Triumph of Surgery, The Thief's Story, The Midnight Visitor, A Question of Trust, Footprints without Feet, The Making of a Scientist, The Necklace, Bholi and The Book That Saved the Earth.
Each story explores human nature, choices, honesty, ambition or social pressure.
Questions often ask for character motivation and the lesson of the story.
Explain and apply Footprints without Feet - Supplementary.

concepts.name: Footprints without Feet - Supplementary
concepts.purpose: Build clear understanding of Footprints without Feet - Supplementary with definitions, examples and exam-style practice.

items.title: Story map: character -> problem -> choice -> consequence -> theme.
Theme web: honesty, greed, courage, education, self-respect, science and curiosity.

keyPoints: The Thief's Story: trust can transform a person.
A Question of Trust: appearances can deceive.
The Necklace: pride and dissatisfaction can be costly.

quickCheck.question: What is the main lesson of 'The Thief's Story'?
quickCheck.explanation: Anil's trust gives Hari Singh a chance to change.

revisionPlan: Write a five-line summary of each story.
Prepare one turning point and one lesson per story.
Practise character-based questions.
Read the Footprints without Feet - Supplementary notes and write five key definitions.
Solve three board-style questions and check every step.
Attempt a timed mixed practice set and review mistakes.

tips: Identify the conflict and the choice the character makes.
Use evidence from the story for every trait.
Link the ending to the theme.
Write the given information and what is asked before solving.
Show every step; board marking rewards reasoning.
Reattempt wrong questions after 24 hours.
